sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other? (No.)** The headline "New sign-ups by channel" (x≈48–370, y≈95–128) and its subtitle only say what the chart is. The chart below shows the same thing again. The message of the piece is in the side note at x≈876–1200, y≈165–350: organic search grew to a third of sign-ups after the guide pages were rewritten, and the events budget moves to referrals. The eye reads that note last, after the title and the bars. So a viewer who glances at this leaves knowing "organic is the biggest". They miss that organic grew, why it grew, and the budget decision. That shift is what the page exists to tell them. Fix: make the headline say the finding, for example "Organic search brought a third of Q3 sign-ups, up from a quarter". Keep the descriptive line as the subtitle. Then the chart works as the evidence for the claim and doesn't just restate the title. If the budget move is the news, pull it nearer the top too. Taste: the source entry is off the approved list, so this is my own judgment. The reason is that the first thing read should carry the point. Weight: major.
2. **Do the colors, shapes, and directions of the piece carry the mood its message calls for? (No.)** The six bars (y≈220–516) use six saturated hues of equal strength: blue, orange, red, green, teal and mauve. The rest of the page is quiet grey and black. The palette feels festive and treats every channel as equally important. The message is a ranking with one winner (organic) and one cut (events). So the color stays neutral about the very point the note makes. The red on Paid social can also read as a warning that isn't meant. Itten, *The Art of Color*: color should support the message, not contradict it. Fix: let color carry the story. Give Organic search one strong hue and the other bars a neutral grey, and perhaps a muted accent on Events to tie it to the budget line. The fact that the colors encode nothing (each bar already has a label) is a chart matter for the data section. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The copy is finished and the numbers agree. The bars sum to the stated 5,400, and 1,840 is 34%, which matches "a third". Podcast plus events comes to 670, which matches "fewer than 700". A reader who checks will trust the page.
- The headings say what their sections hold. "New sign-ups by channel" with "Accounts created in Q3, by the channel of the first visit" sets the scope exactly, including what counts as a channel. "What changed this quarter" plainly labels the note as the interpretation.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (main image and headline make one idea; colors and shapes carry the mood the message calls for)

**Walk (working notes).** The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image. Bash was refused, so I could not run the crop or entries scripts.
First read: the eye lands on the bold black title "New sign-ups by channel", drops to the tall blue Organic search bar, then runs down the colored bars. The side note on the right ("What changed this quarter") is found last.
- One element stands clearly above the rest: yes. The title (about 26 px, bold, near black) is the largest and darkest text on the page.
- Each text level can be told from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same: yes. Title about 26 px, subtitle and side body about 15 px, source line about 13 px. Subtitle and source are set apart by grey color, and the side heading by bold. The 13 and 15 px sizes are close, but color and position separate them.
- Headings that are larger also differ in weight, form, or color: yes. The title is bold. The side heading is the same size as its body but bold, which is the right way to do it.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

One point outside the checklist, for the director to weigh. It is taste and copy, and no checklist line covers it. The order of importance on the page puts the label above the message:
- The title (48–370, 96–128) names a category: "New sign-ups by channel".
- The actual findings sit in the right column (876–1195, 165–350) at body size, below the visual weight of the chart: organic search brought a third of accounts, and the events budget moves to referrals.
- A reader who skims gets "here are six bars" and has to dig to the side to learn what to conclude or what was decided.

Direction: put the main finding in the headline, for example "Organic search now brings a third of sign-ups". Keep "by channel" as the subtitle. Weight: minor to major, depending on whether this page is meant to report or to persuade.

**What's working.**
- **The title owns the page.** It is the clear first stop: the largest, boldest and darkest text, with a lighter grey subtitle right under it. The eye never has to choose where to start.
- **The side note is separated by weight, not size.** "What changed this quarter" is bold at body size, not a bigger competing heading, so it stays below the title and doesn't fight it (Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*: bolder, not bigger).

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** No. The top of the "What changed this quarter" heading in the right column (about x 876, y 166) doesn't line up with anything in the left column. It sits about 30 px below the subtitle (y≈137–153) and about 20–30 px above the top of the chart (the "2,000" label at y≈189, the top gridline at y≈195). It looks like it was meant to line up with the top of the chart and missed. The viewer sees a slightly loose, unfinished join between the two columns instead of one clean top line. Why: Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, says each element should align to a shared edge, and Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, says a placement that is neither clearly here nor clearly there makes the eye waver. The Arnheim point that a break must look deliberate is not confirmed in the reference. Fix: align the cap height of the heading exactly to one shared line. The top gridline or the top of the "2,000" label works if the notes belong to the chart. The subtitle line works if they belong to the page. Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **One left edge.** The logo, title, subtitle and source line all start at x 48, with 48 px margins on both sides of the page. That gives the page one firm left edge and frames the chart and source as one unit.
- **Two-column split.** The chart takes about two-thirds of the width (x 48–808) and the notes about one-third (from x 876), with a clear gutter of about 68 px. The chart clearly leads and the notes read as a commentary on it. The empty space is gathered at the bottom and lower right instead of scattered.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (aligned exactly or clearly off).

I've finished the text checklist walk. The only open line, line length, resolves to yes. Here is the report.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The sidebar sets its points as short sentences.** "What changed this quarter" sits on a narrow side column at x≈876–1200. Each line is about 39 to 43 characters with open leading, which is within Bringhurst's 40 to 50 for text in several columns. Each paragraph is a short, complete statement with a verb and a number to measure it against ("a third… up from a quarter in Q2"; "fewer than 700"). A reader takes it in at one glance and gets no ragged or orphaned lines.
- **One sans family carries every level of text, and size and weight do the work.** The bold heading at about 26 px, the grey subtitle, the bold value labels on the bars, the regular category labels, and the small grey source line at y≈580 are all in that one family. The quieter levels use lighter colour rather than yet another size. The source line looks faint but holds up readable in a close crop.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Color: applies. Outside the chart the page is neutral: white, near-black and mid-grey. The six bar colours are a palette question for the data section and are left to it. This section covers only how the status hues inside the chart read.

**Findings**
1. **Is each status color (red, green, amber, blue) used only for its usual meaning to this audience? No.**
   - **Where:** The bar colours are status hues used as plain category colours. Paid social is red (bar at about x 362–437, y 362–516) and Podcast ads is green (about x 596–670, y 450–516).
   - **What the viewer meets:** This is a growth dashboard, so people expect red to mean "down or bad" and green to mean "up or good". They will read a verdict into these colours that the data doesn't give. Paid social is the third-best channel at 960, yet it is the one painted as a warning. Podcast ads gets "success" green, but the side note at x 876 says it is one of the two channels that together brought fewer than 700 accounts.
   - **Why:** Red marks errors and danger and green marks success, and these colours should not be used for unrelated decoration (Apple *Human Interface Guidelines: Color*; Material Design, colour roles).
   - **Fix direction:** Take red and green out of the category colours. A single neutral or brand hue for all bars, with an accent only on the bar the story is about, removes the false signal. That also matches the data section's restraint question. If the colours must stay categorical, choose hues with no status meaning.
   - **Kind and weight:** Convention. Minor: the labels and values are correct, so nobody is misled about the numbers, only nudged toward the wrong reading of them.

**What's working.**
- Outside the chart the page uses only greys: near-black for the heading and note, mid-grey for the subtitle, source line and nav. Any colour on the page therefore reads as data, and the bold black "Growth" in the nav marks the current page without needing a hue.
- No meaning depends on colour alone. Every bar has its category name underneath and its value on top, so someone with a colour-vision deficiency loses nothing.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 8 yes, 1 no (status colors used only for their usual meaning)

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The page has no photos, illustrations or icons. The only thing that could count as a mark is the "Pebblepost" name at the top left (about 48–148, 18–40 px), and that is set in bold type, not a logo image. It has clear space around it, isn't distorted and uses the page's own ink colour, so nothing about it fails. The bar chart is data, not a picture, and belongs to the Charts and data critic.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped

sections.report:
**Section.** Charts and data: applies (one bar chart of Q3 sign-ups by channel, 6 bars).

**Findings**
1. **Does each chart use few distinct colors for its series or categories, with gray for context?** No. The chart covers x≈128–787 and y≈195–515. It has one series, but each bar has its own saturated colour: blue, orange, red, teal, green, mauve. The colour encodes nothing, because every bar already has a channel name under it. What the viewer gets is a rainbow where every bar shouts equally, and the red Paid social bar looks like a warning when it isn't one. The two points the page actually makes are in the side panel: Organic search is a third of all accounts, and Podcast ads plus Events are the weak pair. Nothing in the chart picks those bars out, so the reader has to match text to bars on their own. Source: Few, "Common Pitfalls in Dashboard Design", pitfall 12; Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*, ch. 19.1. Fix: draw all the bars in one colour, or in grey, and keep one accent colour for the bar the reader must notice (Organic search). If the events-to-referrals move matters, a second muted accent on Podcast ads and Events would tie the chart to the panel text. Convention, with a defect side: it hides the point and adds a false alarm. Weight: **major**, because it decides whether the chart shows the story or just lists the numbers.
2. **Does each headline number come with a comparison, such as a target, the previous period, or a trend?** No. Every value label (1,840; 1,210; …) has its unit and period from the subtitle "Accounts created in Q3", but none has a comparison. The main claim on the page, "up from a quarter in Q2" in the panel at x≈876, y≈206–252, rests on Q2 data that the chart never shows. So the reader takes the change on trust and can't tell whether any other channel grew or shrank. Source: Few, "Common Pitfalls in Dashboard Design", pitfall 2. Fix: put the Q2 value next to each bar, either as a pale paired bar or as a tick mark or "Q2: 1,2xx" note, or give the change next to each value label. Convention. Weight: **minor**. Units and period are present, and the panel states the one key comparison in words. Only the chart lacks it.

**What's working.**
- Honest, readable structure. The bars start at zero, the ticks are even at 500, the gridlines are pale enough to drop back, and the bars are sorted from largest to smallest. Each bar has its exact value on top and its category directly below, so there's no legend and no lookup.
- The numbers add up and back the text. The bars sum to the 5,400 given in the source line. 1,840 is about 34%, which is "a third", and Podcast ads plus Events is 670, which is "fewer than 700". So the caption's claims can be checked against the chart.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 14 yes, 2 no (few colors with gray for context; headline numbers with a comparison)

**Section.** Interface: applies. The only controls are the top nav (Pebblepost wordmark, then Campaigns, Growth, Audience and Billing).

**Findings**
1. **Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?** No. The Growth report under the header (about x 48–808, y 95–590) is fixed to Q3. There is no period picker, no compare-to-previous-quarter toggle, no channel filter and no export. The sidebar (about x 876–1200, y 165–350) builds its argument on a Q2 comparison: "up from a quarter in Q2". A reader who wants to check that, or to see what Q4 looks like after the budget moves, has nothing on this screen to do it with and has to leave the page or ask someone. Nielsen's heuristic 7 (flexibility and efficiency of use) asks for accelerators such as filters on frequent actions, and changing the time range is the most common one in a growth report. Fix direction: if this is a live app page, put a period control by the title (a quarter selector, ideally with "compare to previous quarter"), so the claim about Q2 can be checked here. If it is meant to be a static snapshot, you can ignore this. Convention (Nielsen 7), applied with judgment, because I can't tell whether the page is live or static. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The current section is marked clearly. "Growth" in the top nav (about x 1036–1086, y 28) is set bold and near-black, while its siblings are regular grey. That is one ordinary cue, which is exactly what Nielsen heuristic 1 and Laubheimer's "Menu-Design Checklist" (NN/g) ask for, and it is enough to show the reader where they are. Keep it.
- The header follows web convention: wordmark top-left, section nav top-right, a thin rule below and nothing fixed over the content. A reader knows where everything is without having to learn it.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- I can't see the nav links' focus indicator or hover state. Check in a browser that keyboard focus shows a ring at least 2 px thick with 3:1 contrast.
- I can't tell whether the header is sticky. If it is, check that it doesn't cover focused elements when tabbing down the page.
- Nav hit areas look fine from the text and the roughly 22 px gaps between items, but I couldn't measure the padding. It should be at least 24 px tall.
- Process note: Bash was refused, so I couldn't run `scripts/crop.mjs` or `scripts/entries.mjs`. The image is about one screen (1280×800), so I judged from the whole image. I read the Nielsen 7 entry directly from `references/ux.md`.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 30 yes, 1 no (shortcuts for frequent actions), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured)
